title: AI Risk Management: A Practical Selection and Implementation Guide
description: A practical AI risk management guide for defining intended use, assessing impact, testing model behavior, protecting data, assigning oversight, and monitoring systems after release.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Define the system and intended use
sections.body: Record what the AI system does, who uses it, which decisions it influences, and what it must not be used for. Map the full system, including model provider, prompts, retrieval sources, tools, downstream actions, human review, and data flows. Separate low-impact assistance from use cases that affect eligibility, safety, employment, finances, health, or access to essential services. The risk process should be proportionate to the real-world consequences, not just the model's technical complexity.

sections.title: Create a risk register with owners
sections.body: For each plausible harm, document affected people, likelihood, severity, existing safeguards, residual risk, and the person responsible for mitigation. Include inaccurate output, privacy leakage, discriminatory outcomes, prompt injection, unauthorized tool use, security compromise, overreliance, and service unavailability where relevant. Record decisions and evidence so risk acceptance is explicit. Escalate high-impact risks to legal, security, privacy, and business owners before release.

sections.title: Test with representative scenarios
sections.body: Build an evaluation set that reflects real users, edge cases, ambiguous inputs, adversarial attempts, and the languages or contexts the system will encounter. Measure task quality alongside harmful errors, refusal behavior, data leakage, consistency, and tool-call correctness. Use human review for judgments that cannot be captured reliably by automated scores. Re-run evaluations when prompts, retrieval data, model versions, tools, or user permissions change.

sections.title: Secure data and tool access
sections.body: Minimize the data sent to the model, apply access controls before retrieval, and avoid placing secrets or unnecessary personal data in prompts and logs. Treat retrieved documents and user content as untrusted input. If the model can call tools, enforce authorization and input validation in the tool itself rather than relying on the model to follow instructions. Require confirmation for consequential external actions and restrict the blast radius of credentials available to the system.

sections.title: Design human oversight and fallback
sections.body: Specify which outputs need review, how reviewers see uncertainty and supporting evidence, and how users can challenge or correct a result. A human reviewer needs enough time, context, and authority to disagree; a rubber-stamp step is not an effective safeguard. Define a safe fallback when the model is unavailable or performs poorly, and make it clear when a user is interacting with AI or when output may require verification.

sections.title: Monitor, respond, and reassess
sections.body: Track quality, latency, cost, user feedback, safety incidents, drift, and override rates after launch. Protect monitoring data from unnecessary exposure and make retention rules explicit. Maintain an incident process for disabling a model or tool, notifying affected stakeholders, preserving evidence, and restoring a safe operating mode. Reassess risk on material changes and at a regular cadence; keep a record of limitations, test results, owners, and unresolved risks.
